openingProblem.problem:
In 1935 the League of Nations imposed sanctions on Italy, yet Addis Ababa fell within seven months. In 1938 Britain and France accepted the union of Germany and Austria and gave Germany the Sudetenland. In March 1939 Britain suddenly promised to defend Poland, and in September it went to war, while the United States declared itself neutral.

Why did the responses of the League and the democracies fail to deter Germany and Italy, and what finally changed them?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: did the democracies fail because they lacked power, will, or unity? Give one reason.
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which source or fact changed or confirmed your judgement?

chunks.title: Why did the League fail to stop Italy in Abyssinia?
chunks.body:
When Italy invaded Ethiopia on 3 October 1935, the League of Nations decided that Italy had broken the Covenant and recommended commercial and financial sanctions. The United States, not a member, imposed its own embargo on arms to both sides under its Neutrality Act, but Secretary of State Hull told the League that the US would “follow our course independently” and did not wish to be invited onto any sanctions committee. By November Hull was warning that American exports of oil, copper, trucks and scrap metal to the belligerents were rising.

The decisive question was oil. In December 1935 the British Foreign Secretary, Sir Samuel Hoare, explained why he had resigned. An oil embargo, he said, might force an end to the war if non-member states took a full part, but every report said Italy would treat it as an act of war, and no member state except Britain had taken military precautions. To avoid an isolated war with Italy he had agreed a basis for negotiation with Laval of France in Paris. In January 1936 the US Minister in Switzerland reported that most delegates saw the oil embargo as “the test of strength between the League of Nations and Mussolini”, but that League states would not apply it unless American supplies stopped too.

This matters because the sanctions that were applied were never decisive. Italy carried on, and Addis Ababa fell on 5 May 1936. The United States never recognised Italian sovereignty, but non-recognition did not change the outcome. In 1936 Italy and Germany drew closer after the League's sanctions.

The League failed in Abyssinia because its members feared a wider war more than an Italian victory, and because the most powerful sanction depended on states outside the League. The failure also showed Hitler that collective security would not be enforced.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The League's members would not risk war with Italy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The League did recommend commercial and financial sanctions, so it did act.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Sanctions depended on non-members, especially the United States.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Hull did try to discourage exports of war materials.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the reasons why League sanctions failed to stop Italy in 1935–1936.
To what extent did the United States weaken the League's response to the Abyssinian crisis?
Compare and contrast what two sources reveal about the proposed oil sanction.

useItInAnEssay.claim: League sanctions failed because members would not risk war and the decisive sanction, oil, depended on non-members.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Hoare told the Commons in December 1935 that Italy would treat an oil embargo as an act of war and that only Britain had taken military precautions.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because no state would face war with Italy, the oil embargo was not imposed, and Italy finished the conquest by May 1936.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the League did recommend sanctions, which showed that collective security was not yet dead in 1935.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The League acted, but not with the one measure that might have worked.

chunks.title: How did Britain, France and the United States respond to German expansion, 1936–1938?
chunks.body:
When German troops entered the Rhineland in March 1936, Britain responded with words and procedure. Foreign Secretary Eden told the Commons that Germany had “profoundly shaken confidence” in any future German promise, but that there was “no reason to suppose that the present German action implies a threat of hostilities”. Britain promised to help France or Belgium if they were attacked, referred the matter to the League Council, and said it would examine Hitler's new proposals.

The pattern was repeated in March 1938. Lord Halifax warned the German Foreign Minister about Austria, and the British Ambassador protested against “coercion, backed by force”. Germany replied that Austria was an internal German affair. Chamberlain then told the Commons the “hard fact” that “nothing could have arrested this action by Germany unless we and others with us had been prepared to use force to prevent it”. Three days later Secretary of State Hull warned Americans that isolation was “a fruitful source of insecurity”, but he also said the US would avoid “undesirable political involvements”.

This matters because the democracies recognised each breach but were not prepared to use force. During the Czech crisis of September 1938 Roosevelt appealed to the governments involved to continue negotiating, and on 29 September Germany, Italy, Britain and France signed the Munich agreement, handing the Sudetenland to Germany. Chamberlain told the Commons on 3 October that “the path which leads to appeasement is long and bristles with obstacles”, and he spoke of a great programme of rearmament.

Appeasement was therefore not simply weakness. It rested on the judgement that only force could stop Germany and that Britain and France were not ready to use it, while the United States would offer only principles. But each concession was followed by a larger demand, and in March 1939 the German occupation of the Czech lands showed that Munich had not satisfied Hitler.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The democracies condemned each breach but would not use force.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Britain did promise to help France and Belgium if attacked, so it drew a line at its own treaty partners.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Appeasement was a calculated policy, combined with rearmament.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The occupation of the Czech lands showed that concessions did not satisfy Hitler.

useItInAnEssay.explain: Because they were not prepared, they accepted the Anschluss and then gave Germany the Sudetenland at Munich in September 1938.

useItInAnEssay.judge: Appeasement was the main response, but it was a choice about timing and readiness, not simply a lack of will.

chunks.title: Why did Britain and France abandon appeasement in 1939?
chunks.body:
The German occupation of the Czech lands on 14–15 March 1939 broke the Munich agreement and Hitler's promise that he had no more territorial claims in Europe. Italy invaded Albania on 7 April. These blows, the State Department later wrote, awoke Europe to the danger it faced. On 31 March Chamberlain told the Commons that if Polish independence were clearly threatened and Poland chose to resist, Britain “would feel themselves bound at once to lend the Polish Government all support in their power”, and that France stood in the same position. Guarantees to Greece and Rumania followed, and talks began with the Soviet Union for a common front.

The United States also spoke more plainly, but without commitments. On 14 April Roosevelt asked Hitler and Mussolini for assurances that they would not attack the independent nations of Europe and the Near East, pointing out that “three nations in Europe and one in Africa have seen their independent existence terminated”. Neither dictator replied directly.

This matters because the guarantee to Poland changed the question from whether to resist to when. The Nazi–Soviet Pact of 23 August removed the prospect of a common front with the Soviet Union, and on 1 September Germany invaded Poland. Britain and France declared war on 3 September, in compliance with their obligations to Poland. The same evening Roosevelt told Americans that the United States would remain neutral, though he could not ask every American to “remain neutral in thought”. In November 1939 Congress repealed the arms embargo, so Britain and France could buy American aircraft and munitions.

Appeasement ended in 1939 because Hitler's seizure of non-German territory showed that his aims had no limit, and because British and French leaders now believed resistance had become unavoidable. The Nazi–Soviet Pact made that resistance harder, but it did not change the decision.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The occupation of the Czech lands showed that Hitler's aims had no limit.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Britain's guarantee was limited to Polish independence, not Polish borders.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The United States moved from appeals to support short of war.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The US remained neutral and Congress alone could commit it to war.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the reasons why Britain and France abandoned appeasement in 1939.
To what extent did the United States change its response to German aggression in 1939?
Compare and contrast what two sources reveal about British and American responses to German aggression in 1939.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Britain and France abandoned appeasement because the occupation of the Czech lands showed that Hitler could not be satisfied.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 31 March 1939 Chamberlain told the Commons that Britain would lend Poland “all support in their power” if its independence were threatened.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because the guarantee committed Britain and France in advance, the German invasion of Poland on 1 September led to war on 3 September.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the guarantee did not deter Hitler, especially once the Nazi–Soviet Pact removed the Soviet danger.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The change of policy made war likely rather than preventing it, but it ended the cycle of concessions.

chunks.title: How did the world respond to combined German and Italian aggression in 1940?
chunks.body:
After a quiet winter, the war spread in the spring of 1940. Germany invaded Denmark and Norway on 9 April; Britain and France sent forces to Norway but were pushed back. On 10 May Germany attacked Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, and the British and French troops sent to help them were forced to withdraw from Dunkirk at the end of May.

Roosevelt tried to keep Italy out. On 29 April and again on 14 May he appealed to Mussolini to stay apart from the war. Mussolini replied on 18 May that Italy “is and intends to remain allied with Germany” and “cannot remain absent at a moment in which the fate of Europe is at stake”. On 10 June Italy declared war on France and Britain. That day Roosevelt said at Charlottesville that “the hand that held the dagger has struck it into the back of its neighbor”, and he promised to “extend to the opponents of force the material resources of this Nation”. The US sent the British and French large quantities of aircraft, rifles, artillery and ammunition.

This matters because American support stopped short of war. On 14 June, the day German troops entered Paris, the French Premier, Paul Reynaud, begged Roosevelt for the certainty that the United States would enter the war “within a very short time”. Roosevelt replied that supplies would continue in ever-increasing quantities, but that his statements carried no military commitment, which only Congress could make. On 17 June the French government under Marshal Pétain asked Germany for armistice terms.

The responses of 1940 therefore came too late to save France. Combined aggression was met by British resistance and by American material aid, but not by American military power, which left Britain to fight on alone after June 1940.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Italy joined the war when German victory seemed certain, despite US appeals.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Mussolini also spoke of loyalty to the German alliance.

argumentsThatWork.claim: US aid in 1940 was material, not military.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The repeal of the arms embargo and the speed of deliveries were real help.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate international responses to German and Italian aggression in 1940.
To what extent did the United States change its policy towards the war in Europe in 1940?
Compare and contrast what two sources reveal about American help to France in June 1940.

useItInAnEssay.claim: In 1940 the democracies responded to combined aggression with resistance and material aid, but too late to save France.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 10 June 1940 Roosevelt promised the “material resources of this Nation”, but on 14 June Reynaud's request for American entry into the war was refused.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because only Congress could commit the US to war, France could not be given the certainty it asked for, and on 17 June it sought an armistice.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, American aircraft and munitions did reach the Allies after the arms embargo was repealed in November 1939.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The response changed in scale in 1940 but not in kind: material help, not intervention.

sourceSets.focus: The League, sanctions and the Abyssinian crisis, 1935–1936

provenance.creator: Cordell Hull, US Secretary of State
provenance.sourceType: telegram to the US delegation at Geneva (State Department paraphrase)
provenance.contextNote: The League was preparing sanctions against Italy, which had invaded Ethiopia on 3 October 1935.

sources.text: For ourselves it should be more and more clear that we have used all our influence and support for the preservation of peace; that now we take the position that we are determined that war shall not involve us; that in pursuance of this policy we will not overlook any possible step that would be consistent with our position. Considering our policy as evidenced by what we have already done and said, with the complete support of American public opinion, we regard it advisable in every respect for the League to understand that definite measures have already been taken by the United States in accordance with our own limitations and policies; that these measures include long steps in restricting commercial and financial transactions with the belligerents; and that we desire to follow our course independently according as circumstances develop. … it would appear not only unnecessary but at this time inadvisable from the viewpoint of this government to invite us to join in any committee organized to consider sanctions.

provenance.creator: Italian photographer (the print carries the mark of the Istituto Luce)
provenance.contextNote: A military parade of Italian troops in Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, with Somali ascari (colonial soldiers) in the background.

provenance.creator: Sir Samuel Hoare, who had just resigned as British Foreign Secretary
provenance.sourceType: personal explanation to the House of Commons
provenance.contextNote: Hoare had agreed proposals for a settlement with Laval of France in Paris; when they became public, he resigned.

sources.text: In both these fields, in both the field of collective action and also in the field of peaceful negotiations, we reached a turning point about a fortnight ago. … It seemed clear that, supposing an oil embargo were to be imposed and that the non-member States took an effective part in it, the oil embargo might have such an effect upon the hostilities as to force their termination. Just because of the effectiveness of the oil sanction, provided that the non-member States had a full part in it, the situation immediately became more dangerous from the point of view of Italian resistance. From all sides we received reports that no responsible Government could disregard that Italy would regard the oil embargo as a military sanction or an act involving war against her. … It was a moment when, while most member States had taken a part in the economic sanctions, no member State except ourselves had taken any military precautions.

provenance.creator: Hugh Wilson, US Minister in Switzerland
provenance.sourceType: private letter to the US Secretary of State, after a meeting of the League Council

sources.text: I cannot conceal from myself the belief that the actual application of an embargo on petroleum by the League States will be dependent largely upon the decision of the United States Congress in respect to the Neutrality legislation. … I doubt whether the embargo will be applied by the League States unless they feel that in some way the supply from the United States will not replace that which they cut off. The reverse also appears true. If the United States curtails its shipments, the States of the League will feel it not only expedient, but morally imperative to put on the embargo. … Suffice it to say that in the minds of most of the Delegates, it is the test of strength between the League of Nations and Mussolini and must be established as a precedent for use against Germany, if necessity arises.

questions.text: According to Source A, what was the US position on League sanctions against Italy?

points: The US was determined that war should not involve it.
It had already taken its own measures, restricting trade and finance with the belligerents.
It would follow its course independently.
It did not wish to be invited to join any sanctions committee.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about the outcome of the Abyssinian crisis by May 1936?

points: Italy had won: its troops were parading in the Ethiopian capital.
Italy used colonial troops, showing the scale of its empire in East Africa.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying the failure of League sanctions against Italy.

points: Value (origin): the British Foreign Secretary who handled the crisis explains, days later, why Britain hesitated over the oil embargo.
Value (content): it shows the central dilemma: oil might end the war, but Italy would treat it as an act of war and only Britain had taken military precautions.
Limitation (purpose): a personal explanation defending himself after resigning, so it stresses the dangers and may play down the concessions offered to Italy.
Limitation (content): it gives the British view only and cannot show how France or Italy judged the risks.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources C and D reveal about the proposed oil sanction against Italy.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources see the oil embargo as decisive: Source C says it might “force their termination”, and Source D calls it “the test of strength between the League of Nations and Mussolini”.
Both also see that it depended on states outside the League: C says it would work “provided that the non-member States had a full part in it”, and D that it depended largely on the US Congress.
However, Source C stresses the danger, that Italy would treat the embargo as an act of war, while Source D stresses the opportunity, a precedent “for use against Germany”.
Source C points to Britain's isolation among League members, whereas Source D suggests League states would feel it “morally imperative” to act if the US cut its shipments.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the reasons why League sanctions failed to stop Italian expansion in Abyssinia in 1935–1936.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: League sanctions failed because members would not risk war over the one decisive measure, oil, and because that measure depended on non-members.
Sources C and D show the dilemma: an oil embargo might end the war, but Italy would treat it as an act of war, and League states would not act unless US supplies stopped too.

Source A shows why US supplies did not stop: the US acted independently under its Neutrality Act, with an arms embargo on both sides from 5 October 1935; in November Hull warned that exports of oil and other war materials were rising.
The result is shown in Source B: Addis Ababa fell on 5 May 1936. Hoare's attempt to negotiate with Laval cost him his post, and in October 1936 Italy and Germany signed a treaty of friendship.
The League acted against Italy, but not decisively, because its leading members feared war more than an Italian victory.

sourceSets.focus: Responses to German expansion: the Rhineland, Austria and Munich, 1936–1938

provenance.creator: Eden, British Foreign Secretary
provenance.sourceType: statement in the House of Commons
provenance.contextNote: German troops had entered the demilitarised Rhineland on 7 March 1936.

sources.text: Let us not delude ourselves. The course taken by the German Government in unilaterally repudiating obligations into which they have freely entered and in simultaneously acting as if they did not exist both complicates and aggravates the international situation. The abrogation of the Locarno Treaty and the occupation of the demilitarised zone have profoundly shaken confidence in any engagement into which the Government of Germany may in future enter. … There is, I am thankful to say, no reason to suppose that the present German action implies a threat of hostilities. … should there take place … any actual attack upon France or Belgium which would constitute a violation of Article II of Locarno, His Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom, notwithstanding the German repudiation of the Treaty, would regard themselves as in honour bound to come in the manner provided in the Treaty to the assistance of the country attacked.

provenance.creator: German picture agency (Scherl Bilderdienst)
provenance.contextNote: Munich. From left: Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler, Mussolini and the Italian Foreign Minister, Ciano.

provenance.creator: Chamberlain, British Prime Minister
provenance.sourceType: statement in the House of Commons
provenance.contextNote: German troops had entered Austria after Germany threatened invasion; the union of Germany and Austria was proclaimed on 13 March 1938.

sources.text: Late on 11th March our Ambassador in Berlin registered a protest in strong terms with the German Government against such use of coercion, backed by force, against an independent State in order to create a situation incompatible with its national independence. … The hard fact is—and of its truth every hon. Member can judge for himself—that nothing could have arrested this action by Germany unless we and others with us had been prepared to use force to prevent it. I imagine that according to the temperament of the individual the events which are in our minds to-day will be the cause of regret, of sorrow, perhaps of indignation. They cannot be regarded by His Majesty's Government with indifference or equanimity. They are bound to have effects which cannot yet be measured. The immediate result must be to intensify the sense of uncertainty and insecurity in Europe.

provenance.creator: Cordell Hull, US Secretary of State
provenance.contextNote: The address was given four days after the union of Germany and Austria was proclaimed.

sources.text: The crucial issue today is whether these principles will be vitalized and be firmly established as the foundation of an international order or whether international anarchy based on brute force will inundate the world and ultimately sweep away the very bases of civilization and progress. That issue is universal. … I stated clearly that we are fully determined to avoid the extremes either of internationalism or of isolationism. Internationalism would mean undesirable political involvements; isolationism would either compel us to confine all activities of our people within our own frontiers, with incalculable injury to the standard of living and the general welfare of our people, or else expose our nationals and our legitimate interests abroad to injustice or outrage wherever lawless conditions arise.

questions.text: According to Source A, what were the consequences of the German action in the Rhineland?

points: It complicated and aggravated the international situation.
It profoundly shook confidence in any future German engagement.
It did not, Eden believed, imply a threat of hostilities.
Britain would still help France or Belgium if they were attacked.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about the Munich Conference?

points: The leaders of Britain, France, Germany and Italy settled the crisis together.
Czechoslovakia, whose territory was at stake, is not shown among the leaders.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying British responses to the Anschluss.

points: Value (origin): the Prime Minister's statement to Parliament gives the government's official account two days after the event.
Value (content): it reveals the reasoning behind appeasement: only force could have stopped Germany, and Britain was not prepared to use it.
Limitation (purpose): Chamberlain was justifying inaction to MPs, so he presents the outcome as unavoidable.
Limitation (content): it shows Britain's view, not France's or Austria's, and gives no evidence of whether force was in fact considered.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources C and D reveal about British and American responses to the Anschluss.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources condemn force: Source C reports a protest against “coercion, backed by force”, and Source D warns against “international anarchy based on brute force”.
Both expect a more dangerous world: C foresees “uncertainty and insecurity in Europe”, and D a threat to “the very bases of civilization and progress”.
However, Source C speaks directly of Germany and Austria, while Source D names no country and speaks in general principles.
Source C concludes that only force could have stopped Germany, whereas Source D rules out “undesirable political involvements”, so the US offered principles without commitments.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent was appeasement the main response of Britain and France to German expansion between 1936 and 1938?

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: Appeasement was the main response of Britain and France in 1936–1938, but it was combined with protests, limited guarantees and rearmament.

Source A shows the Rhineland response: condemnation, a promise to help France or Belgium if attacked, and referral to the League Council, but no force. Source C shows the same over Austria: protests, then acceptance because only force could have stopped Germany.

Source B shows appeasement at its height: at Munich on 29 September 1938 the Sudetenland was handed to Germany. On 3 October Chamberlain called appeasement a long path that “bristles with obstacles” and spoke of rearmament.
Source D shows that the United States offered only principles, which left Britain and France without American support; Roosevelt's appeals in September 1938 asked only for continued negotiation.
Appeasement was the main response, but it was a calculated choice by powers that judged they were not ready to fight, and it ended when Germany occupied the Czech lands in March 1939.

sourceSets.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
sourceSets.focus: The end of appeasement and the outbreak of war, 1939

provenance.creator: Chamberlain, British Prime Minister
provenance.sourceType: statement in the House of Commons
provenance.contextNote: German troops had occupied the Czech lands two weeks earlier.

sources.text: I am glad to take this opportunity of stating again the general policy of His Majesty's Government. They have constantly advocated the adjustment, by way of free negotiation between the parties concerned, of any differences that may arise between them. … As the House is aware, certain consultations are now proceeding with other Governments. In order to make perfectly clear the position of His Majesty's Government in the meantime before those consultations are concluded, I now have to inform the House that during that period, in the event of any action which clearly threatened Polish independence, and which the Polish Government accordingly considered it vital to resist with their national forces, His Majesty's Government would feel themselves bound at once to lend the Polish Government all support in their power. They have given the Polish Government an assurance to this effect. I may add that the French Government have authorised me to make it plain that they stand in the same position in this matter as do His Majesty's Government.

provenance.creator: Clifford Berryman, American cartoonist
provenance.sourceType: cartoon published in The Washington Star
provenance.contextNote: Hitler and Stalin as a bride and groom. The caption reads: “Wonder how long the honeymoon will last?”

provenance.creator: Roosevelt, US President
provenance.sourceType: telegram to Hitler (an identical message was sent to Mussolini)
provenance.contextNote: The message was also made public.

sources.text: You realize I am sure that throughout the world hundreds of millions of human beings are living today in constant fear of a new war or even a series of wars. … It is, however, unfortunately necessary to take cognizance of recent facts. Three nations in Europe and one in Africa have seen their independent existence terminated. A vast territory in another independent nation of the Far East has been occupied by a neighboring state. Reports, which we trust are not true, insist that further acts of aggression are contemplated against still other independent nations. Plainly the world is moving toward the moment when this situation must end in catastrophe unless a more rational way of guiding events is found. You have repeatedly asserted that you and the German people have no desire for war. If this is true there need be no war.

provenance.creator: Roosevelt, US President
provenance.sourceType: radio address to the American people
provenance.contextNote: Britain and France had declared war on Germany that day.

sources.text: Until 4:30 this morning I had hoped against hope that some miracle would prevent a devastating war in Europe and bring to an end the invasion of Poland by Germany. … This Nation will remain a neutral nation, but I cannot ask that every American remain neutral in thought as well. Even a neutral has a right to take account of facts. Even a neutral cannot be asked to close his mind or his conscience. I have said not once but many times that I have seen war and that I hate war. I say that again and again. I hope the United States will keep out of this war. I believe that it will. And I give you assurances that every effort of your Government will be directed toward that end.

questions.text: According to Source A, what did Britain promise Poland?

points: If an action clearly threatened Polish independence, and Poland chose to resist, Britain would support Poland at once.
Britain would lend Poland “all support in their power”.
The assurance applied while consultations with other governments went on.
France stood in the same position as Britain.

questions.text: What is the message of Source B?

points: The alliance between Hitler and Stalin is an unnatural match.
It is unlikely to last.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying international responses to German aggression in 1939.

points: Value (origin): a message from the US President to Hitler shows the American government's response at the highest level.
Value (content): its list of independent nations “terminated” shows that by April 1939 the US saw a pattern of aggression, not isolated incidents.
Limitation (purpose): it was published to influence world opinion, so it is an appeal, not a statement of what the US would do.
Limitation (content): it commits the US to nothing, so it cannot show whether the US was willing to act; neither dictator replied directly.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and D reveal about British and American responses to German aggression in 1939.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources show leaders who had hoped for a peaceful settlement: Source A says Britain “constantly advocated” free negotiation, and in Source D Roosevelt “hoped against hope” that war could be avoided.
Both also respond to German action against Poland: A to a threat to “Polish independence”, D to “the invasion of Poland by Germany”.
However, Source A commits Britain in advance to “all support in their power” if Poland resists, while Source D declares that the United States “will remain a neutral nation”.
Source A is a promise made with France before war, whereas Source D is a public reassurance made after war had begun, aimed at keeping the US out.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate the responses of the democracies to German aggression in 1939.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: In 1939 Britain and France moved from appeasement to resistance, while the United States moved from appeals to neutrality with sympathy; neither change deterred Hitler.
After the occupation of the Czech lands on 14–15 March, Source A shows Britain and France guaranteeing Polish independence; guarantees to Greece and Rumania and talks with the Soviet Union followed.

Source C shows Roosevelt's appeal for assurances, which neither dictator answered directly. The Nazi–Soviet Pact of 23 August, mocked in Source B, ended the hope of a common front with the Soviet Union.

When Germany invaded Poland, Britain and France declared war on 3 September, but Source D shows the US remaining neutral. In November 1939 the arms embargo was repealed so Britain and France could buy American arms.
The responses were firmer than in 1938 but came too late to deter Germany; their value was that Germany could no longer expand without war.

provenance.creator: Roosevelt, US President
provenance.sourceType: address at the University of Virginia, Charlottesville
provenance.contextNote: Italy had declared war on France and Britain that day.

sources.text: The Government of Italy has now chosen to preserve what it terms its “freedom of action” and to fulfill what it states are its promises to Germany. In so doing it has manifested disregard for the rights and security of other nations, disregard for the lives of the peoples of those nations which are directly threatened by this spread of the war; and has evidenced its unwillingness to find the means through pacific negotiations for the satisfaction of what it believes are its legitimate aspirations. On this tenth day of June 1940, the hand that held the dagger has struck it into the back of its neighbor. … in our American unity, we will pursue two obvious and simultaneous courses; we will extend to the opponents of force the material resources of this Nation and, at the same time, we will harness and speed up the use of those resources in order that we ourselves in the Americas may have equipment and training equal to the task of any emergency and every defense.

provenance.creator: Gutjahr, German army war reporter
provenance.contextNote: German troops parading past their generals at the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, on the day they entered the city.

provenance.creator: Benito Mussolini, head of the Italian government
provenance.contextNote: Roosevelt had asked Mussolini on 14 May to “stay wholly apart from any war”. Germany had attacked Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands on 10 May.

sources.text: I reply to the message which you sent me at noon on the fourteenth instant. I understand perfectly the motives by which it was inspired and I consider it worthy of much respect and of the greatest consideration but there are two fundamental motives which cannot escape your spirit of political realism and those are that Italy is and intends to remain allied with Germany and that Italy cannot remain absent at a moment in which the fate of Europe is at stake. I cannot therefore but reconfirm the substance of my first message.

provenance.creator: Paul Reynaud, Premier of France
provenance.contextNote: “Then” refers to Reynaud's earlier appeal of 10 June 1940.

sources.text: I told you then that for six days and six nights our troops had been fighting without an hour of respite, and at one against three, with war material five times less powerful. Four days of bloody fighting have gone by since then. Our army is now cut into several parts. Our divisions are decimated. … The Reichswehr has just entered Paris. … At the most tragic hour of its history France must choose. … From that time on France can continue the struggle only if American intervention reverses the situation by making an Allied victory certain. … I know that the declaration of war does not depend on you alone. But I must tell you at this hour, so grave in our history as in yours, that if you cannot give to France in the hours to come the certainty that the United States will come into the war within a very short time, the fate of the world will change.

questions.text: According to Source A, how had Italy acted, and how would the United States respond?

points: Italy had disregarded the rights and security of other nations.
It had refused to seek its aims through peaceful negotiation.
Roosevelt said Italy had struck a dagger into the back of its neighbour.
The US would extend its material resources to the opponents of force while building its own defences.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about the situation of France on 14 June 1940?

points: Germany had taken Paris and was displaying its victory at a national monument.
French resistance in the capital had ended.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying Italy's entry into the war.

points: Value (origin): Mussolini's own reply to the US President records the reasons he gave at the time.
Value (content): it shows that by 18 May he had decided Italy would not stay out, naming loyalty to the German alliance and the fate of Europe.
Limitation (purpose): a short diplomatic reply meant to end the exchange politely, so it hides Italy's own territorial aims.
Limitation (content): it does not say when Italy would act, or show the influence of German victories in France and the Low Countries.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and D reveal about American help to France in June 1940.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources show that American help was central to the Allies' hopes: Source A promises “the material resources of this Nation”, and Source D says France can continue only through “American intervention”.
Both describe the crisis as grave: A condemns the spread of the war, and D speaks of “the most tragic hour” of France's history.
However, Source A offers material aid only, while Source D asks for the certainty that the United States will “come into the war within a very short time”.
Source A also stresses American defence (“equipment and training equal to the task of any emergency”), whereas Source D warns that without US entry “the fate of the world will change”.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate international responses to German and Italian aggression in 1940.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: International responses in 1940 were too limited and too late to stop combined German and Italian aggression, though they kept Britain in the war.
Britain and France fought: they sent forces to Norway in April and to the Low Countries in May, but were pushed back and had to withdraw from Dunkirk.

The United States tried diplomacy and aid: Roosevelt appealed to Mussolini, but Source C shows Italy's refusal, and Italy entered the war on 10 June. Source A shows the US offering material resources, and it sent aircraft, rifles, artillery and ammunition.

Source D shows the limit: France needed American entry into the war, which Roosevelt said only Congress could decide. Source B shows the result: German troops in Paris on 14 June; on 17 June France asked for an armistice.
The responses could not save France, but American material aid prepared the way for continued resistance by Britain.
